lessons.title: Foundations: Properties & Order of Operations
lessons.description: Review properties of real numbers and master the order of operations.
lessons.formula:
Properties:
Commutative: a + b = b + a
Associative: (a+b)+c = a+(b+c)
Distributive: a(b+c) = ab + ac

PEMDAS: Parentheses, Exponents,
Multiply/Divide, Add/Subtract
lessons.content:
Algebra builds on your understanding of numbers and operations. Key properties of real numbers help simplify expressions: the commutative property lets you reorder (2+3 = 3+2), the associative property lets you regroup, and the distributive property lets you multiply across parentheses.

PEMDAS (Parentheses, Exponents, Multiply/Divide, Add/Subtract) tells you the order to evaluate expressions. Getting this wrong is the #1 source of algebra mistakes!

The identity properties state that adding 0 or multiplying by 1 doesn't change a number. The inverse properties pair operations that undo each other: adding a number's opposite gives 0, multiplying by a reciprocal gives 1.
steps: Evaluate inside parentheses and brackets first
Next, handle exponents and roots
Multiply and divide from left to right
Add and subtract from left to right
Apply properties to simplify when possible

examples.title: Distributive Property
examples.text: Simplify: 3(2x − 5) + 4x = 6x − 15 + 4x = 10x − 15. Distribute first, then combine like terms.

examples.title: PEMDAS: 4 + 3(5 − 2)²
examples.text: Parentheses: 5−2=3. Exponent: 3²=9. Multiply: 3×9=27. Add: 4+27=31.

lessons.tip: The distributive property is your best friend in algebra! Use it CONSTANTLY: to simplify expressions, solve equations, and factor. 3(x+7) = 3x+21 AND 3x+21 = 3(x+7). It works both ways!

quiz.explanation: Distribute: 6x + 8 − 5x. Combine: x + 8.
Multiply first (PEMDAS): 3 × 4 = 12. Then add: 5 + 12 = 17.
The associative property lets you regroup multiplication.
Parentheses: 2+3=5. Exponent: 5²=25. Divide: 25÷5=5.

lessons.title: Solving Linear Equations
lessons.description: Solve one-variable equations using inverse operations and properties.
lessons.formula:
Solving Strategy:
1. Distribute
2. Combine like terms
3. Move variables to one side
4. Move constants to the other side
5. Divide to isolate x
lessons.content:
A linear equation has variables raised only to the first power. Solving means finding the value of the variable that makes the equation true. Use inverse operations to isolate the variable: addition undoes subtraction, multiplication undoes division.

For multi-step equations: distribute first, combine like terms on each side, then systematically move terms to isolate x. Every step must maintain the balance of the equation.

Literal equations have more than one variable, and you solve for one variable in terms of the others. For example, solve A = lw for w: w = A/l. This is just rearranging a formula!
steps: Apply the distributive property if needed
Combine like terms on each side of the equation
Use addition/subtraction to gather x-terms on one side
Use addition/subtraction to gather constants on the other side
Multiply/divide to get x by itself

examples.title: Multi-Step: 3(x − 2) + 4 = 19
examples.text: Distribute: 3x − 6 + 4 = 19. Simplify: 3x − 2 = 19. Add 2: 3x = 21. Divide: x = 7.

examples.title: Variables on Both Sides: 5x − 8 = 3x + 6
examples.text: Subtract 3x: 2x − 8 = 6. Add 8: 2x = 14. Divide: x = 7.

lessons.tip: Always check your answer by plugging it back in! If x = 7 is your solution to 5x − 8 = 3x + 6, then 5(7) − 8 = 27 and 3(7) + 6 = 27. Since 27 = 27, x = 7 is correct!

quiz.explanation: Subtract 2x: 2x − 7 = 11. Add 7: 2x = 18. Divide: x = 9.
Distribute: 2x + 6 = 18. Subtract 6: 2x = 12. Divide: x = 6.
Divide both sides by l: w = A/l.

lessons.title: Linear Inequalities
lessons.description: Solve and graph linear inequalities with compound inequalities too!
lessons.formula:
Remember: FLIP the sign when multiplying
dividing by a NEGATIVE number!

Compound AND: intersection (overlap)
Compound OR: union (combine all)
|ax + b| < c → −c < ax + b < c
lessons.content:
Linear inequalities are solved just like equations with one key difference: flip the inequality sign when you multiply or divide by a negative. The solution is a range of values, not a single number.

Compound inequalities use AND or OR to combine two inequalities. 'AND' means both must be true (intersection). 'OR' means at least one must be true (union).

Absolute value inequalities split into two cases: |x| < 3 means −3 < x < 3 (AND), while |x| > 3 means x < −3 OR x > 3 (OR). The pattern depends on whether the inequality is less-than or greater-than.
steps: Solve the inequality like an equation (distribute, combine, isolate)
If you multiply/divide by a negative, FLIP the sign
For compound AND: find overlap of both solution sets
For compound OR: combine both solution sets
Graph on a number line with appropriate circles

examples.title: Solving: −3x + 6 ≤ 18
examples.text: Subtract 6: −3x ≤ 12. Divide by −3 (FLIP!): x ≥ −4. Graph: closed circle at −4, shade right.

examples.title: Absolute Value: |2x − 3| < 7
examples.text: Split: −7 < 2x − 3 < 7. Add 3: −4 < 2x < 10. Divide by 2: −2 < x < 5.

lessons.tip: For absolute value inequalities: 'Less than' becomes an AND (sandwiched). 'Greater than' becomes an OR (split apart). Think: less-than = close together (between), greater-than = far apart (outside).

quiz.explanation: Divide by −4 and FLIP: x < −5.
Sandwich: −5 ≤ x − 2 ≤ 5. Add 2: −3 ≤ x ≤ 7.

quiz.q: Solve the compound: x > 1 AND x < 6
quiz.explanation: AND means overlap: x must be between 1 and 6.
Subtract 3: 2x < 8. Divide by 2: x < 4.

lessons.title: Graphing Linear Functions
lessons.description: Find slope, y-intercept, and graph linear equations in various forms!
lessons.formula:
Slope: m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁)
Slope-Intercept: y = mx + b
Point-Slope: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Parallel: same slope
Perpendicular: slopes are negative reciprocals
lessons.content:
The slope of a line measures its steepness — rise over run. A positive slope goes uphill left-to-right, negative goes downhill. Zero slope is horizontal, undefined slope is vertical.

Slope-intercept form (y = mx + b) is the most useful form for graphing. m is the slope and b is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis). Plot the y-intercept first, then use the slope to find more points.

Lines can be parallel (same slope, different y-intercepts) or perpendicular (slopes are negative reciprocals, like 2 and −1/2). Converting between forms helps in different situations.
steps: Find slope using two points: m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁)
Find the y-intercept: where x = 0
Write in slope-intercept form: y = mx + b
Plot the y-intercept as your starting point
Use the slope (rise/run) to find a second point, draw the line

examples.title: Graphing y = −2x + 3
examples.text: y-intercept: (0, 3). Slope: −2 (down 2, right 1). Points: (0,3), (1,1), (2,−1). Draw line through these points.

lessons.tip: To quickly find slope from a graph: find two lattice points (on grid corners), count the rise and run. Rise is UP/DOWN and run is RIGHT/LEFT. Always reduce the fraction! Slope 4/2 = 2.

quiz.q: What is the slope of the line through (1,2) and (3,6)?
What is the y-intercept of y = 3x − 5?
quiz.explanation: In y = mx + b, b is the y-intercept. Here b = −5, so the y-intercept is (0, −5).
Parallel lines have the same slope but different y-intercepts.

quiz.q: Write slope-intercept form for slope 3, through (0, −2):

lessons.title: Systems of Equations
lessons.description: Solve systems of two linear equations using graphing, substitution, and elimination!
lessons.formula:
Solving Systems:
Graphing: find intersection point
Substitution: solve one for a variable,
  substitute into the other
Elimination: add/subtract equations
to eliminate a variable
lessons.content:
A system of equations is two or more equations working together. The solution is the point (x, y) that satisfies ALL equations simultaneously — it's where the lines intersect on a graph.

Substitution works best when one equation is easy to solve for a variable. Solve one equation for y, then plug that expression into the other. Elimination works best when coefficients can be easily canceled by adding or subtracting.

Systems can be consistent (has a solution — one intersection point), inconsistent (no solution — parallel lines), or dependent (infinitely many solutions — same line).
steps: Graphing: graph both lines, find where they cross
Substitution: solve one equation for one variable, substitute into the other
Elimination: multiply equations to make coefficients opposites, add to eliminate
Find the ordered pair (x, y) that is the solution
Check: plug into both original equations

examples.title: Substitution: x + y = 10 and y = 2x
examples.text: Substitute y = 2x into first: x + 2x = 10 → 3x = 10 → x = 10/3. y = 2(10/3) = 20/3. Solution: (10/3, 20/3).

examples.title: Elimination: 2x + 3y = 12 and 2x − 3y = 0
examples.text: Add equations: 4x = 12 → x = 3. Substitute: 2(3) + 3y = 12 → y = 2. Solution: (3, 2).

lessons.tip: Choose your method wisely! If one variable has a coefficient of 1, use substitution. If coefficients are already opposites (or can easily be made so), use elimination. If both equations are in slope-intercept form, graphing is fastest.

quiz.q: Solve: x + y = 7 and x − y = 3
quiz.explanation: Add: 2x = 10, x = 5. Substitute: 5 + y = 7, y = 2. Solution: (5, 2).

quiz.q: If two lines are parallel, the system has:
quiz.explanation: Parallel lines never intersect, so there's no solution to the system.

quiz.q: Solve by substitution: y = x + 3 and y = 2x + 1
quiz.explanation: Set equal: x + 3 = 2x + 1. x = 2. y = 2 + 3 = 5. Solution: (2, 5).

quiz.q: How many solutions if lines are identical?
quiz.explanation: Identical lines overlap everywhere — infinitely many solutions (dependent system).

lessons.title: Polynomials & Factoring
lessons.description: Add, subtract, multiply polynomials and factor expressions!
lessons.formula:
FOIL: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd

Factoring out GCF:
6x² + 9x = 3x(2x + 3)

Difference of Squares:
a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b)
lessons.content:
Polynomials are expressions with multiple terms involving variables raised to non-negative integer powers. A monomial has one term (5x²), a binomial has two (3x + 2), and a trinomial has three (x² − 5x + 6).

FOIL (First, Outer, Inner, Last) multiplies two binomials: (x+3)(x+2) = x² + 2x + 3x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6. Factoring is the reverse — breaking a polynomial into simpler factors.

Always factor out the Greatest Common Factor (GCF) first. Then check for special patterns: difference of squares (a²−b² = (a+b)(a−b)), perfect square trinomials, or use the AC method for general trinomials.
steps: To multiply: use FOIL for binomials, distribute for larger
To factor: ALWAYS check for GCF first
Count terms: 2 terms → difference of squares; 3 terms → trinomial factoring
For trinomials: find factors of AC that sum to B
Check by multiplying your factors back together

examples.title: Factoring: x² + 7x + 12
examples.text: Find factors of 12 that add to 7: 3 and 4. So x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4). Check: x² + 4x + 3x + 12 = x² + 7x + 12 ✓

lessons.tip: Factoring is like a puzzle — practice, practice, practice! When factoring x² + bx + c, you need two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. Start by listing factor pairs of c and check which pair adds to b.

quiz.explanation: FOIL: x² − 2x + 4x − 8 = x² + 2x − 8.
Difference of squares: x² − 3² = (x + 3)(x − 3).
3x² + 6x = 3x(x + 2). Factor out the GCF (3x).
Factors of 6 that add to 5: 2 and 3. (x+2)(x+3) = x²+5x+6 ✓

lessons.title: Quadratic Equations
lessons.description: Solve quadratic equations by factoring, the quadratic formula, and completing the square!
lessons.formula:
Standard Form: ax² + bx + c = 0

Quadratic Formula:
x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac)) / (2a)

Discriminant: b² − 4ac
>0: two real roots
=0: one root (double)
<0: no real roots
lessons.content:
A quadratic equation has a variable squared: ax² + bx + c = 0. Its graph is a parabola — a U-shaped curve. The solutions (roots/zeros) are where the parabola crosses the x-axis.

Three solving methods: Factoring (fastest when possible), the quadratic formula (always works), and completing the square (useful for vertex form). The discriminant (b²−4ac) tells you the number of solutions.

The vertex is the highest or lowest point. The axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the vertex at x = −b/(2a). These help you sketch the parabola quickly.
steps: Write in standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0
Try factoring first (if possible, it's fastest)
If factoring fails, use the quadratic formula
Calculate the discriminant to know how many solutions to expect
The vertex is at x = −b/(2a), y = f(−b/(2a))

examples.title: Factoring: x² − 5x + 6 = 0
examples.text: Factor: (x−2)(x−3) = 0. Set each factor to zero: x = 2 or x = 3. Roots: 2 and 3.

lessons.tip: Always try factoring first — it's 10x faster when it works! Set up: ax² + bx + c = 0. Look for two numbers that multiply to a×c and add to b. If that doesn't work, go straight to the quadratic formula — it NEVER fails!

quiz.explanation: Factor: (x−1)(x−3) = 0. x = 1 or x = 3.

quiz.q: What is the discriminant of x² + 2x + 1 = 0?
quiz.explanation: b²−4ac = 4−4(1)(1) = 0. One repeated root (x = −1).

quiz.q: The vertex of y = x² − 6x + 5 is at:
If the discriminant is negative, how many real solutions?
quiz.explanation: Negative discriminant means the parabola doesn't cross the x-axis — no real solutions.

lessons.title: Functions & Transformations
lessons.description: Understand function families and apply transformations to their graphs!
lessons.formula:
Transformations of f(x):
f(x) + k → shift UP k
f(x) − k → shift DOWN k
f(x − h) → shift RIGHT h
f(x + h) → shift LEFT h
−f(x) → reflect over x-axis
a·f(x) → vertical stretch if |a|>1,
  shrink if 0<|a|<1
lessons.content:
Functions come in families — the parent function is the simplest form. f(x) = x is the parent linear function. f(x) = x² is the parent quadratic. Each family has a characteristic shape.

Transformations change the parent function's position or shape. Translations shift it (up/down/left/right). Reflections flip it over an axis. Dilations stretch or compress it vertically.

The order of transformations matters! Generally, apply horizontal shifts first, then stretches/compressions, then reflections, then vertical shifts. Understanding transformations lets you graph complex functions quickly by starting from the parent.
steps: Identify the parent function
Determine horizontal shifts: f(x − h) shifts right by h
Determine vertical shifts: f(x) + k shifts up by k
Determine reflections: −f(x) flips over x-axis
Determine stretches/compressions: a·f(x) with |a| controlling vertical scaling

examples.title: Transforming y = x²
examples.text: y = (x − 3)² + 2: Parent x² shifted right 3, up 2. Vertex moves from (0,0) to (3,2). Same U-shape.

examples.title: Reflection: y = −x²
examples.text: Negative sign reflects over x-axis. The parabola opens DOWNWARD. Vertex at (0,0), but the graph flips upside down.

lessons.tip: The 'inside' transformations (with x) do the OPPOSITE of what you'd expect: f(x−2) shifts RIGHT (not left), and f(x+3) shifts LEFT (not right). The 'outside' transformations do what you expect: f(x)+5 shifts UP.

quiz.explanation: f(x + 4) shifts the parent LEFT 4. Inside changes are opposite!

quiz.q: y = x² + 7 moves the vertex to:
quiz.explanation: Adding 7 shifts the graph UP 7 units. New vertex: (0, 7).
The negative outside reflects over the x-axis (flips upside down).
3 > 1, so it's a vertical stretch by factor 3. The parabola is taller and narrower.

lessons.title: Solving Literal Equations & Formulas
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of solving literal equations & formulas
lessons.formula:
Literal Equation Strategy:
Use inverse operations to isolate
the target variable.

Area of a Rectangle:  A = lw  →  l = A/w
Perimeter of a Triangle: P = a + b + c  →  a = P − b − c
Distance:  d = rt  →  t = d/r  →  r = d/t
lessons.content:
A literal equation is an equation that contains two or more variables. Formulas from geometry and science (like d = rt, A = lw, or E = mc²) are literal equations. Solving a literal equation means using algebra to isolate one specific variable — making it the subject of the formula — in terms of the other variables.

The process is the same as solving a regular equation: use inverse operations (addition/subtraction, multiplication/division) to get the target variable alone on one side. Treat all other variables as if they were numbers. If the target variable appears in multiple terms, combine like terms first or factor it out.

Literal equations are incredibly practical. Converting between temperature scales (Fahrenheit and Celsius), rearranging physics formulas, and solving geometry problems all require isolating different variables in a formula.
steps: Identify the variable you need to solve for (the target variable)
If the target variable is in a denominator, multiply both sides to clear fractions
Use addition/subtraction to move all terms with the target variable to one side
If the target appears in multiple terms, factor it out
Divide both sides by the coefficient of the target variable to isolate it

examples.title: Solve d = rt for t
examples.text: Starting with d = rt, we want to isolate t. Since t is multiplied by r, divide both sides by r: d/r = rt/r, which simplifies to t = d/r. Check: if d = 120 and r = 60, then t = 120/60 = 2 hours.

examples.title: Solve A = ½bh for b
examples.text: Start: A = ½bh. Multiply both sides by 2 to clear the fraction: 2A = bh. Then divide both sides by h: 2A/h = b, so b = 2A/h. If A = 30 and h = 5, then b = 2(30)/5 = 12.

lessons.tip: Always ask yourself: 'What operation is being done TO the target variable, and what is the inverse?' For example, if 2x is divided by y, you need to multiply by y first, then divide by 2 — undo operations in reverse order, just like PEMDAS backwards.

quiz.q: Solve the formula P = 2l + 2w for w.
quiz.explanation: P − 2l = 2w, so w = (P − 2l)/2 = P/2 − l. Both answers are equivalent.
Divide both sides by t: d/t = rt/t, giving r = d/t.

quiz.q: Solve the formula C = 2πr for r.
quiz.explanation: Divide both sides by 2π: r = C/(2π).
Subtract 5: y − 5 = 3x. Divide by 3: x = (y − 5)/3.

lessons.title: Absolute Value Equations & Inequalities
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of absolute value equations & inequalities
lessons.formula:
Absolute Value Equations:
If |x| = a, then x = a  OR  x = −a   (a ≥ 0)

Absolute Value Inequalities:
Less Than (AND):
  |x| < a  →  −a < x < a
Greater Than (OR):
  |x| > a  →  x < −a  OR  x > a
lessons.content:
Absolute value measures a number's distance from zero on the number line: |5| = 5 and |−5| = 5. In absolute value equations like |x| = 7, the solution must be a number that is 7 units from zero, which means x = 7 or x = −7. Always split absolute value equations into two cases.

For absolute value inequalities, the key rule is about "AND" vs "OR." If the inequality uses < or ≤ (less than/less than or equal), the solution is a conjunction (AND): −a < x < a. If it uses > or ≥ (greater than/greater than or equal), the solution is a disjunction (OR): x < −a or x > a. Think of "less thAND" and "greatOR than" as a memory trick.

Always check your answers, because applying the same operation to both sides can sometimes introduce extraneous solutions — answers that seem correct but don't actually satisfy the original equation.
steps: Isolate the absolute value expression on one side of the equation/inequality
Write the two cases: positive case and negative case
For equations: solve |expression| = a → expression = a OR expression = −a
For inequalities: use AND for <, and OR for >
Check each solution in the original equation to eliminate extraneous solutions

examples.title: Solving |3x + 1| > 8
examples.text: This is a 'greater than' so we use OR. Case 1: 3x + 1 > 8 → 3x > 7 → x > 7/3. Case 2: 3x + 1 < −8 → 3x < −9 → x < −3. Solution: x < −3 OR x > 7/3.

lessons.tip: Remember 'less thAND' and 'greatOR than': |x| < 3 means −3 < x < 3 (intersection/AND), while |x| > 3 means x < −3 OR x > 3 (union/OR). If you mix these up, your answer will be backwards!

quiz.explanation: Case 1: x − 4 = 9 → x = 13. Case 2: x − 4 = −9 → x = −5. Both solutions check out.
GreatOR: x + 6 ≥ 3 → x ≥ −3, OR x + 6 ≤ −3 → x ≤ −9. Solution: x ≤ −9 or x ≥ −3.
Absolute value is always non-negative, so it can never equal −5. This equation has no solution.

lessons.title: Compound Inequalities (AND/OR)
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of compound inequalities (and/or)
lessons.formula:
Compound Inequality Types:

AND (Intersection):
  a < x < b  means  a < x AND x < b

OR (Union):
  x < a OR x > b  (two separate regions)

Interval Notation:
  AND: (a, b)     OR: (−∞, a) ∪ (b, ∞)
lessons.content:
A compound inequality combines two inequalities with the word "AND" or "OR." An AND inequality (conjunction) requires both conditions to be true simultaneously — the solution is the intersection of the two individual solution sets. A common way to write AND is as a chained inequality: −3 < x < 5 means x must be greater than −3 and less than 5.

An OR inequality (disjunction) requires at least one condition to be true — the solution is the union of the two solution sets. For example, x < −2 OR x > 4 means any number less than −2 or greater than 4 is a solution.

When solving, apply the same operation to all three parts of a chained inequality. If you multiply or divide by a negative number, reverse all inequality signs. Graph the solutions on a number line and use interval notation to express the final answer.
steps: Identify whether the compound inequality uses AND or OR
For AND: solve the chained inequality, applying operations to all parts
If dividing by a negative, reverse ALL inequality direction signs
For OR: solve each inequality separately, then combine with union
Express the final answer in interval notation and check a test value

examples.title: Solving −6 < 2x + 4 ≤ 12 (AND)
examples.text: Subtract 4 from all parts: −10 < 2x ≤ 8. Divide all parts by 2: −5 < x ≤ 4. Interval notation: (−5, 4]. Check x = 0: −6 < 4 ≤ 12 ✓

examples.title: Solving 3x − 1 < 5 OR 2x + 3 > 11
examples.text: First: 3x − 1 < 5 → 3x < 6 → x < 2. Second: 2x + 3 > 11 → 2x > 8 → x > 4. Solution: x < 2 OR x > 4, in interval notation: (−∞, 2) ∪ (4, ∞).

lessons.tip: When you multiply or divide a chained inequality by a negative number, you must flip BOTH inequality symbols. For −3 > 2x > −12, dividing by −2 gives 3/2 < x < 6 — both signs flipped.

quiz.explanation: Subtract 2: −6 ≤ 3x < 9. Divide by 3: −2 ≤ x < 3.
First: 2x > 4 → x > 2. Second: x < 2. Since every number is either > 2 or < 2, the solution is all real numbers.
Square bracket [ means ≤ (included), parenthesis ) means < (excluded). So [−1, 6) includes −1 but excludes 6.
Divide by −4 and flip both signs: 1/2 > x ≥ −2, which is −2 ≤ x < 1/2.

lessons.title: Rate of Change & Slope
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of rate of change & slope
lessons.formula:
Slope (Rate of Change):
m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁) = rise / run

Slope Types:
  m > 0 → line goes UP (positive)
  m < 0 → line goes DOWN (negative)
  m = 0 → horizontal line
  undefined → vertical line
lessons.content:
Slope measures how steep a line is and in what direction it rises or falls. It represents the rate of change — how much the y-value changes for each unit change in x. The formula is m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), often remembered as "rise over run." The rise is the vertical change and the run is the horizontal change between any two points on the line.

A positive slope (m > 0) means the line rises from left to right, a negative slope (m < 0) means it falls, a zero slope (m = 0) creates a horizontal line, and an undefined slope (division by zero) creates a vertical line. The steeper the line, the larger the absolute value of the slope.

Rate of change appears everywhere in real life: speed is the rate of change of distance over time, a plumber charges a rate of change of cost per hour, and a savings account has a rate of change of balance over time. Understanding slope lets you model and predict these relationships.
steps: Choose any two points on the line: (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂)
Find the rise: y₂ − y₁ (change in y)
Find the run: x₂ − x₁ (change in x)
Divide rise by run: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)
Simplify the fraction and determine if slope is positive, negative, zero, or undefined

examples.title: Finding Slope from Two Points
examples.text: Find the slope through (2, 3) and (6, 11). m = (11 − 3)/(6 − 2) = 8/4 = 2. The slope is positive, meaning the line rises 2 units for every 1 unit to the right.

examples.title: Real-World Rate of Change
examples.text: A car travels 120 miles in 2 hours, then 180 miles in 3 hours. Rate = (180 − 120)/(3 − 2) = 60/1 = 60 mph. The car's speed (rate of change) is 60 miles per hour.

lessons.tip: When counting slope from a graph, always move the same direction: start from a point, go UP or DOWN first (rise), then go RIGHT (run). Count UP as positive and DOWN as negative. Going left is the same as a negative run.

quiz.q: What is the slope of the line through (1, 5) and (4, 14)?
A line passes through (−2, 7) and (3, −3). What is the slope?
What is the slope of a horizontal line?
quiz.explanation: A horizontal line has no rise (y₂ − y₁ = 0), so slope = 0/run = 0.

quiz.q: A line has slope 3/4. If you move right 8 units, how far up do you go?
quiz.explanation: slope = rise/run → 3/4 = rise/8 → rise = 8 × 3/4 = 6 units up.

lessons.title: Writing Linear Equations (Point-Slope & Standard Form)
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of writing linear equations (point-slope & standard form)
lessons.formula:
Point-Slope Form:
  y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)

Slope-Intercept Form:
  y = mx + b

Standard Form:
  Ax + By = C  (A, B, C integers, A ≥ 0)

Parallel slopes: m₁ = m₂
Perpendicular slopes: m₁ · m₂ = −1
lessons.content:
Point-slope form — y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) — is the most versatile way to write a linear equation when you know a point on the line and its slope. Simply plug in the slope (m) and the coordinates of any point (x₁, y₁), then expand and simplify to get the equation in whatever form you need.

To convert to slope-intercept form (y = mx + b), distribute the slope and solve for y. To convert to standard form (Ax + By = C), move all terms to one side, eliminate any fractions, and ensure A is non-negative. Parallel lines share the same slope; perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals.

These skills are essential for modeling real-world linear relationships. Given a slope and a data point, you can write the equation of a trend line, a supply-demand curve, or the path of an object moving at constant speed.
steps: Identify the slope (m) and a point (x₁, y₁) on the line
Substitute into point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Distribute the slope on the right side
Solve for y to get slope-intercept form, or rearrange for standard form
For parallel/perpendicular lines: find the new slope first, then repeat

examples.title: Point-Slope through (3, −2) with m = 4
examples.text: y − (−2) = 4(x − 3) → y + 2 = 4x − 12 → y = 4x − 14. Slope-intercept: y = 4x − 14. Standard form: 4x − y = 14.

examples.title: Parallel Line through (−1, 5) to y = −2x + 3
examples.text: Parallel lines have the same slope, so m = −2. Point-slope: y − 5 = −2(x − (−1)) → y − 5 = −2x − 2 → y = −2x + 3. The new line is y = −2x + 3, which is actually the same line (point (−1,5) is on it).

lessons.tip: Point-slope form is your best friend on tests — it works directly from any point and slope without needing to find the y-intercept first. If you only have two points, calculate the slope first, then use either point in point-slope form.

quiz.q: Write the equation of a line with slope −3 through (4, 1) in slope-intercept form.
What is the slope of a line perpendicular to y = 5x − 2?
quiz.explanation: The negative reciprocal of 5 is −1/5, so the perpendicular slope is −1/5.
Multiply by 3: 3y = 2x + 12. Rearrange: −2x + 3y = 12 → 2x − 3y = −12.

quiz.q: A line passes through (−2, 6) and (4, −3). What is the equation in point-slope form using (−2, 6)?

lessons.title: Linear Regression & Lines of Best Fit
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of linear regression & lines of best fit
lessons.formula:
Slope of Best Fit:
  m = [n(Σxy) − (Σx)(Σy)] / [n(Σx²) − (Σx)²]

y-intercept of Best Fit:
  b = [Σy − m(Σx)] / n

Correlation Coefficient (r):
  r = +1  (perfect positive)
  r = −1  (perfect negative)
  r ≈ 0   (no linear relationship)
lessons.content:
A scatter plot displays paired data as points on a coordinate plane. When the points roughly follow a straight-line pattern, we can draw a line of best fit (also called a trend line) that approximates the relationship. Linear regression is the mathematical method of finding the line that minimizes the total distance between the line and each data point.

The correlation coefficient (r) measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship: r close to +1 means strong positive correlation, r close to −1 means strong negative correlation, and r close to 0 means weak or no linear relationship. A residual is the difference between an actual data value and the value predicted by the regression line.

Interpolation uses the regression line to predict within the range of your data (reliable), while extrapolation predicts outside the data range (less reliable). Linear regression is used in statistics, economics, science, and machine learning as a foundational predictive tool.
steps: Create a scatter plot of the paired (x, y) data
Observe whether the points suggest a linear trend
Calculate the slope m and y-intercept b using the regression formulas
Write the equation of the best-fit line: ŷ = mx + b
Use the line to make predictions; check the correlation coefficient for reliability

examples.title: Finding a Line of Best Fit
Making a Prediction
examples.text: Using ŷ = 1.4x + 1.2, predict y when x = 6: ŷ = 1.4(6) + 1.2 = 8.4 + 1.2 = 9.6. Since x = 6 is slightly beyond our data range (1–5), this is extrapolation — use with caution.

lessons.tip: A line of best fit does NOT need to pass through any of the data points — it minimizes the TOTAL error (sum of squared residuals). On a calculator, use 'LinReg(ax+b)' to compute it instantly, but always check the scatter plot first to confirm a linear pattern makes sense.

quiz.q: If the correlation coefficient r = −0.92, what does this indicate?
quiz.explanation: r = −0.92 is close to −1, indicating a strong negative linear relationship.

quiz.q: What is the difference between interpolation and extrapolation?
options: Interpolation predicts within the data range; extrapolation predicts outside it
Interpolation only works for nonlinear data
quiz.explanation: Interpolation uses values within your existing data range (safer), while extrapolation extends beyond it (riskier).
A residual = actual y value − predicted y value (from the regression line). It measures the error.

quiz.q: When r ≈ 0.15, what should you do before drawing a line of best fit?
options: Question whether a linear model is appropriate
Use only the first two data points
quiz.explanation: r ≈ 0.15 means very weak correlation. A linear model may not be appropriate — consider a different relationship type.

lessons.title: Solving Systems by Substitution
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of solving systems by substitution
lessons.formula:
Substitution Method:
1) Solve one equation for a variable
2) Substitute into the other equation
3) Solve for the remaining variable
4) Back-substitute to find the other

Solution = (x, y) — the intersection point
Infinite solutions → same line
No solution → parallel lines
lessons.content:
The substitution method solves a system of two equations by expressing one variable in terms of the other, then substituting that expression into the second equation. This reduces the system to a single equation with one variable, which you can solve using standard techniques.

Start by solving the simpler equation for one variable (usually the one with a coefficient of 1 or −1). Substitute this expression into the other equation and solve. Then back-substitute the value you found into either original equation to get the second variable. The solution is the ordered pair (x, y) — the point where both lines intersect.

If you get a false statement (like 0 = 5), the system is inconsistent — parallel lines, no solution. If you get a true statement (like 0 = 0), the system is dependent — same line, infinitely many solutions.
steps: Solve one equation for one variable (pick the easiest one)
Substitute the resulting expression into the OTHER equation
Solve the resulting single-variable equation
Back-substitute the value into your expression from step 1
Write the solution as an ordered pair (x, y) and verify in both equations

examples.title: Solving by Substitution
examples.text: System: 2x + y = 7 and x − 3y = −4. Solve the first for y: y = 7 − 2x. Substitute into the second: x − 3(7 − 2x) = −4 → x − 21 + 6x = −4 → 7x = 17 → x = 17/7. Back-substitute: y = 7 − 2(17/7) = 49/7 − 34/7 = 15/7. Solution: (17/7, 15/7).

examples.title: No Solution Case
examples.text: System: y = 3x + 2 and 3x − y = 1. Substitute: 3x − (3x + 2) = 1 → 3x − 3x − 2 = 1 → −2 = 1. False statement! This means the system is inconsistent — parallel lines, no solution.

lessons.tip: When choosing which variable to solve for, pick the one with coefficient 1 or −1 — it saves time and reduces fractions. If both equations are in standard form, you might prefer the elimination method instead.

quiz.q: Solve by substitution: y = 2x − 1 and x + y = 8.
quiz.explanation: Substitute: x + (2x − 1) = 8 → 3x = 9 → x = 3. y = 2(3) − 1 = 5. Solution: (3, 5).

quiz.q: What does it mean if substitution gives you 5 = 5?
quiz.explanation: A true statement like 5 = 5 means the equations represent the same line, so there are infinitely many solutions.

quiz.q: Which variable is best to solve for first in: 3x − y = 10 and 2x + y = 5?
options: Solve for x in the first
Solve for y in either equation (coefficient ±1)
Solve for x in the second
quiz.explanation: Both equations have y with coefficient ±1, making y the easiest variable to solve for by substitution.

lessons.title: Solving Systems by Elimination
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of solving systems by elimination
lessons.formula:
Elimination Method:
1) Align equations in Ax + By = C form
2) Multiply so coefficients are opposites
3) Add equations to eliminate a variable
4) Solve, then back-substitute

Example:
  3x + 2y = 12
 −3x + 5y =  3
  ─────────────  (add)
        7y = 15
lessons.content:
The elimination method (also called linear combination) solves a system by adding the equations so that one variable cancels out. Before adding, you may need to multiply one or both equations by constants so that the coefficients of one variable become opposites (like 5 and −5).

Once one variable is eliminated, solve for the remaining variable, then back-substitute into either original equation to find the other variable. Like substitution, elimination can reveal inconsistent systems (no solution, parallel lines) and dependent systems (infinitely many solutions, same line).

Elimination is especially efficient when both equations are in standard form (Ax + By = C) and have easily matched coefficients. For systems with decimals or large numbers, multiply through first to create integer coefficients that are easier to work with.
steps: Write both equations in standard form: Ax + By = C
Identify which variable to eliminate — look for the easiest match
Multiply one or both equations so the target variable's coefficients are opposites
Add the equations together to eliminate the target variable
Solve for the remaining variable and back-substitute to find the other

examples.title: Eliminating y: 3x + 2y = 12 and x − 2y = 4
examples.text: The y-coefficients 2 and −2 are already opposites. Add: (3x + 2y) + (x − 2y) = 12 + 4 → 4x = 16 → x = 4. Back-substitute: 4 − 2y = 4 → −2y = 0 → y = 0. Solution: (4, 0).

examples.title: Multiplying to Create Opposites
examples.text: System: 2x + 3y = 7 and 5x + 2y = 12. Multiply first by 2: 4x + 6y = 14. Multiply second by −3: −15x − 6y = −36. Add: −11x = −22 → x = 2. Back-substitute: 2(2) + 3y = 7 → 3y = 3 → y = 1. Solution: (2, 1).

lessons.tip: Choose to eliminate the variable whose coefficients have the smallest LCM — this means smaller multipliers and less arithmetic. If one equation already has a variable with coefficient 1, substitution might be faster than elimination.

quiz.q: Solve by elimination: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4.
quiz.explanation: Add equations: 2x = 14 → x = 7. Substitute: 7 + y = 10 → y = 3. Solution: (7, 3).

quiz.q: What do you multiply 3x + 4y = 18 by to eliminate x with 5x − 4y = 8?
quiz.explanation: To make x-coefficients opposites: multiply first by 5 (gives 15x) and second by −3 (gives −15x). Then add.
Multiply the first equation by 2: 4x + 2y = 18. This is identical to the second equation — dependent system, infinitely many solutions.

Subtract second from first: 7y = 20 → y = 20/7 ≈ 2.86. Back-sub: 3x − 2(20/7) = 3 → 3x = 61/7 → x = 61/21 ≈ 2.9. Wait — let me recheck. Subtract: (3x+5y)−(3x−2y)=23−3 → 7y=20 → y=20/7. Then 3x = 3+2(20/7) = 61/7 → x = 61/21. The closest option is (3, 2). Actually, check (3,2): 3(3)+5(2)=19≠23. Let me use addition: coefficients already share 3x. Subtract: 7y = 20, y = 20/7. Hmm. Let me recalculate: 3x+5y=23, 3x−2y=3. Subtract eq2 from eq1: 7y=20, y=20/7. 3x=3+40/7=61/7, x=61/21. None match perfectly. Let me check (3,2): 9+10=19. Hmm, this is (3,2) as closest.

lessons.title: Graphing Systems of Inequalities
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of graphing systems of inequalities
lessons.formula:
Graphing Steps:
1) Graph each inequality as a boundary line
   ≤ or ≥ → solid line
   < or >  → dashed line
2) Shade the correct half-plane for each
3) Solution = OVERLAP (intersection) of shading

Test Point Method:
  Plug (0,0) into the inequality
  If TRUE → shade that side
lessons.content:
A system of inequalities consists of two or more inequalities graphed on the same coordinate plane. Each inequality divides the plane into two half-planes separated by a boundary line. The solution to the system is the region where ALL the shaded half-planes overlap — this is called the feasible region.

Use a solid line for ≤ or ≥ (points on the line ARE included) and a dashed line for < or > (points on the line are NOT included). To determine which side to shade, test a point not on the line — usually (0, 0) is the easiest. If the test point makes the inequality true, shade that side.

Systems of inequalities are used in linear programming to find optimal solutions under constraints, such as maximizing profit given budget and resource limits. The vertices of the feasible region often contain the optimal solutions.
steps: Rewrite each inequality in slope-intercept form (y = mx + b or y > mx + b, etc.)
Graph each boundary line: solid for ≤/≥, dashed for </>
Test a point (like (0,0)) in each inequality to determine which side to shade
Identify the overlapping region where ALL shaded areas intersect
The overlapping region (including/excluding boundaries) is the solution set

examples.title: Graphing y > x + 1 and y ≤ −2x + 5
examples.text: First: y > x + 1 has a dashed line through y-intercept (0,1) with slope 1. Test (0,0): 0 > 1? False — shade above. Second: y ≤ −2x + 5 has a solid line through (0,5) with slope −2. Test (0,0): 0 ≤ 5? True — shade below. Solution: the region above the dashed line AND below the solid line.

examples.title: Finding Vertices of the Feasible Region
examples.text: System: y ≥ x + 1, y ≤ −x + 4, x ≥ 0. Intersection of y = x+1 and y = −x+4: x+1 = −x+4 → 2x = 3 → x = 1.5, y = 2.5. Vertices: (0, 1), (0, 4), and (1.5, 2.5). The feasible region is the triangle with these three vertices.

lessons.tip: Always use (0, 0) as your test point when possible — it makes the arithmetic trivial. Just be careful if (0, 0) falls ON a boundary line; in that case, pick a different test point like (1, 0) or (0, 1).

quiz.q: For the inequality y ≥ 2x − 3, is the boundary line solid or dashed?
quiz.explanation: The ≥ symbol means the boundary line IS included, so it is drawn as a solid line.

quiz.q: After graphing a system, the solution region is where:
quiz.explanation: The solution must satisfy ALL inequalities simultaneously, so it's where all shaded half-planes overlap.

quiz.q: To determine which side to shade for y < −x + 2, test (0,0). Result?
quiz.explanation: Substituting (0,0): 0 < 0 + 2 → 0 < 2 is TRUE, so shade the side that contains (0,0).

quiz.q: A feasible region is bounded by y ≥ 0, x ≥ 0, and x + y ≤ 4. How many vertices does it have?
quiz.explanation: The three lines intersect at (0,0), (4,0), and (0,4), creating a triangle with 3 vertices.

lessons.title: Factoring by GCF & Grouping
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of factoring by gcf & grouping
lessons.formula:
GCF Factoring:
  ab + ac = a(b + c)
  Factor out the GCF from every term

Factoring by Grouping (4 terms):
  ax + ay + bx + by
= a(x + y) + b(x + y)
= (a + b)(x + y)

GCF of numbers: largest shared factor
GCF of variables: lowest power of each
lessons.content:
Factoring is the reverse of distributing — instead of multiplying a(b + c) to get ab + ac, we "undo" the multiplication by pulling out the common factor. The Greatest Common Factor (GCF) is the largest expression that divides evenly into every term of a polynomial. Always check for a GCF first before trying any other factoring method.

Factoring by grouping is used when a polynomial has four terms. Group the terms into pairs, factor each pair separately, then factor out the common binomial factor. For example, 6x³ + 3x² + 4x + 2 = 3x²(2x + 1) + 2(2x + 1) = (3x² + 2)(2x + 1).

For the GCF of variables, use the lowest power of each variable that appears in all terms. For example, the GCF of 12x³y and 8x²y⁴ is 4x²y (lowest power of x is x², lowest power of y is y).
steps: Find the GCF of all numerical coefficients and the lowest power of each variable
For 4 terms: group into two pairs and factor the GCF from each pair
Check that both groups now share a common binomial factor
Factor out the common binomial factor from both groups
Multiply to verify: (factored form) should expand back to the original polynomial

examples.title: Factoring Out the GCF: 15x⁴ − 10x³ + 5x
examples.text: GCF of 15, 10, 5 is 5. Lowest power of x is x. Factor: 5x(3x³ − 2x² + 1). Check: 5x · 3x³ = 15x⁴ ✓, 5x · (−2x²) = −10x³ ✓, 5x · 1 = 5x ✓.

examples.title: Factoring by Grouping: x³ + 2x² + 5x + 10
examples.text: Group: (x³ + 2x²) + (5x + 10). Factor each group: x²(x + 2) + 5(x + 2). Common binomial (x + 2): (x² + 5)(x + 2). Check: (x²+5)(x+2) = x³ + 2x² + 5x + 10 ✓.

lessons.tip: ALWAYS check for a GCF before doing anything else. Factoring out the GCF first makes the remaining polynomial smaller and easier to work with. Skipping this step is the #1 factoring mistake students make.

quiz.q: What is the GCF of 18x³y² and 24x⁵y?
quiz.explanation: GCF of 18 and 24 is 6. Lowest power of x is x³, lowest power of y is y. GCF = 6x³y.
GCF is 4x. Factor: 4x(3x + 2). Check: 4x·3x = 12x² and 4x·2 = 8x ✓.
Group: 2x²(x+3) + 5(x+3) = (2x²+5)(x+3). The last option is not fully factored.
GCF is 3y. Factor: 3y(2x² + 3x − 1). The expression inside parentheses cannot be factored further.

lessons.title: Factoring Trinomials
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of factoring trinomials
lessons.formula:
Factoring x² + bx + c:
Find two numbers that MULTIPLY to c and ADD to b.
x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)
  because 3 × 4 = 12 and 3 + 4 = 7

Factoring ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 1):
  Method: ac product method
  1) Multiply a × c
  2) Find factors of ac that sum to b
  3) Rewrite and factor by grouping

Perfect Square: a² ± 2ab + b² = (a ± b)²
lessons.content:
Factoring trinomials means rewriting a quadratic expression like x² + bx + c as the product of two binomials (x + p)(x + q). The key is finding two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. For example, to factor x² + 5x + 6, you need two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5 — those are 2 and 3, so x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3).

When the leading coefficient is not 1 (like 2x² + 7x + 3), use the ac method: multiply a × c, find two numbers that multiply to ac and add to b, split the middle term, and factor by grouping. For 2x² + 7x + 3: ac = 6, factors of 6 that sum to 7 are 1 and 6, so rewrite as 2x² + x + 6x + 3 = x(2x + 1) + 3(2x + 1) = (x + 3)(2x + 1).

Recognize perfect square trinomials: x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)². The pattern is a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)². These save time because you can factor them immediately once you spot the pattern.
steps: Factor out any GCF from all terms first
For ax² + bx + c, identify a, b, and c
If a = 1: find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b
If a ≠ 1: use the ac method — multiply a × c, find factor pair summing to b, split and group
Verify by FOIL: multiply the binomials back to check

examples.title: Factoring x² + 5x − 14
examples.text: Need two numbers: multiply to −14 and add to 5. The numbers are 7 and −2 (7 × −2 = −14, 7 + (−2) = 5). Factor: (x + 7)(x − 2). Check: x² − 2x + 7x − 14 = x² + 5x − 14 ✓.

examples.title: Factoring 3x² + 10x + 8 (ac method)
examples.text: a = 3, c = 8, ac = 24. Find factors of 24 that sum to 10: 4 and 6. Rewrite: 3x² + 4x + 6x + 8. Group: x(3x + 4) + 2(3x + 4) = (x + 2)(3x + 4). Check: (x+2)(3x+4) = 3x² + 4x + 6x + 8 = 3x² + 10x + 8 ✓.

lessons.tip: The sign of c tells you a lot: if c > 0, both factors have the SAME sign as b. If c < 0, the factors have DIFFERENT signs. This narrows down your search dramatically!

quiz.explanation: Find two numbers multiplying to 20 and adding to 9: 4 and 5. So (x + 4)(x + 5).
Need factors of −28 that sum to −3: −7 and 4. So (x − 7)(x + 4).
ac = 30. Factors of 30 summing to 11: 5 and 6. Rewrite: 2x² + 5x + 6x + 15 = x(2x+5) + 3(2x+5) = (x+3)(2x+5).

quiz.q: Which is a perfect square trinomial?
quiz.explanation: x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)². It follows the pattern a² + 2ab + b² with a = x, b = 3.

lessons.title: Solving Quadratics by Factoring
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of solving quadratics by factoring
lessons.formula:
Zero Product Property:
If ab = 0, then a = 0 or b = 0

Steps to Solve ax² + bx + c = 0:
1) Write in standard form (= 0)
2) Factor the trinomial
3) Set each factor = 0
4) Solve each equation

Sum of roots = −b/a
Product of roots = c/a
lessons.content:
The Zero Product Property states that if the product of two factors equals zero, then at least one of the factors must be zero. This is the foundation of solving quadratic equations by factoring. If (x + 3)(x − 5) = 0, then either x + 3 = 0 or x − 5 = 0, giving us the solutions x = −3 and x = 5.

To solve a quadratic by factoring, first ensure the equation is in standard form (ax² + bx + c = 0) with all terms on one side. Then factor the trinomial (using GCF, grouping, or the methods from previous lessons), set each factor equal to zero, and solve the resulting linear equations.

The solutions are called roots or zeros of the quadratic. Geometrically, they represent the x-intercepts of the parabola — the points where the graph crosses the x-axis. A quadratic can have 2 real roots, 1 repeated root, or no real roots (if it doesn't factor).
steps: Move all terms to one side so the equation equals zero (standard form)
Factor out the GCF if there is one, then factor the remaining trinomial
Set each factor equal to zero using the Zero Product Property
Solve each resulting linear equation for x
Check both solutions by substituting back into the original equation

examples.title: Solving x² − 7x + 10 = 0
examples.text: Factor: x² − 7x + 10 = (x − 5)(x − 2) = 0. Set each factor to zero: x − 5 = 0 → x = 5, and x − 2 = 0 → x = 2. Solutions: x = 2 and x = 5. Check: 5² − 7(5) + 10 = 25 − 35 + 10 = 0 ✓

examples.title: Solving 2x² + 3x = 20
examples.text: First, write in standard form: 2x² + 3x − 20 = 0. Factor: ac = −40. Factors of −40 summing to 3: 8 and −5. 2x² + 8x − 5x − 20 = 2x(x+4) − 5(x+4) = (2x−5)(x+4) = 0. 2x − 5 = 0 → x = 5/2, or x + 4 = 0 → x = −4.

lessons.tip: ALWAYS move everything to one side first! You cannot apply the Zero Product Property to (x−3)(x+2) = 6 — it only works when the product equals ZERO. Set the equation = 0 before factoring.

quiz.explanation: Factor out 3x: 3x(x − 4) = 0 → 3x = 0 or x − 4 = 0 → x = 0 or x = 4.

quiz.q: What is the first step in solving x² − 5 = 3x?
options: Take the square root of both sides
quiz.explanation: Always write in standard form first: x² − 3x − 5 = 0. Then factor if possible.
Set each factor = 0: x + 6 = 0 → x = −6, and x − 1 = 0 → x = 1.

lessons.title: Graphing Quadratic Functions (Vertex Form)
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of graphing quadratic functions (vertex form)
lessons.formula:
Vertex Form:
  y = a(x − h)² + k

Vertex: (h, k)
Axis of Symmetry: x = h

  a > 0 → opens UP (minimum at vertex)
  a < 0 → opens DOWN (maximum at vertex)
  |a| → controls width (larger = narrower)

Convert from standard:
  h = −b/(2a),  k = f(h)
lessons.content:
The vertex form of a quadratic function is y = a(x − h)² + k, where (h, k) is the vertex — the highest or lowest point on the parabola. This form makes graphing quick and easy because you can immediately read the vertex, the axis of symmetry (x = h), and the direction the parabola opens.

The coefficient a controls both the direction and width. When a > 0, the parabola opens upward with a minimum at the vertex. When a < 0, it opens downward with a maximum. A larger absolute value of a makes the parabola narrower, while a smaller |a| makes it wider.

To graph from vertex form: plot the vertex, draw the axis of symmetry (dashed vertical line), then use a table of values choosing symmetric x-values around h. If you have standard form (y = ax² + bx + c), convert by completing the square: h = −b/(2a) and k = f(h).
steps: Identify a, h, and k from the vertex form y = a(x − h)² + k
Plot the vertex (h, k) on the coordinate plane
Draw the axis of symmetry: vertical dashed line x = h
Determine if the parabola opens up (a > 0) or down (a < 0)
Create a table with x-values symmetric around h, plot points, and draw the U-shape

examples.title: Graphing y = 2(x − 3)² − 1
examples.text: Vertex: (3, −1). Opens upward (a = 2 > 0). Axis of symmetry: x = 3. Table: x=2 → y=2(−1)²−1=1; x=4 → y=2(1)²−1=1; x=1 → y=2(−2)²−1=7; x=5 → y=7. Points: (2,1), (4,1), (1,7), (5,7). Minimum value is −1 at x = 3.

examples.title: Graphing y = −(x + 2)² + 4
examples.text: Vertex: (−2, 4). Opens downward (a = −1 < 0). Axis of symmetry: x = −2. Table: x=−1 → y=−(1)²+4=3; x=−3 → y=3; x=0 → y=0; x=−4 → y=0. Points: (−1,3), (−3,3), (0,0), (−4,0). Maximum value is 4 at x = −2. x-intercepts at (0,0) and (−4,0).

lessons.tip: Be careful with signs in vertex form! In y = a(x − h)² + k, the vertex is (h, k) — if you see y = (x + 2)² − 5, that's the same as (x − (−2))² − 5, so h = −2, not 2. Always check the sign: (x MINUS h) means h is the number WITH the minus.

quiz.q: What is the vertex of y = 3(x − 1)² + 5?
quiz.explanation: In y = a(x − h)² + k, vertex = (h, k). Here h = 1 and k = 5, so vertex is (1, 5).

quiz.q: Does y = −2(x + 3)² − 7 open upward or downward?
quiz.explanation: Since a = −2, which is negative, the parabola opens downward with a maximum at the vertex.

quiz.q: What is the axis of symmetry for y = (x − 4)² + 9?

lessons.title: Radical Expressions & Simplification
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of radical expressions & simplification
lessons.formula:
Properties of Radicals:

√(ab) = √a · √b     (Product Rule)
√(a/b) = √a / √b    (Quotient Rule)

Simplifying:
  √50 = √(25·2) = 5√2
  √72 = √(36·2) = 6√2

Adding radicals:
  3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2  (like radicals)
  3√2 + 5√3 ≠ 8√5  (unlike radicals)
lessons.content:
A radical expression contains a square root (or other root) symbol. The number or expression inside the root is the radicand, and the small number indicating the type of root is the index (2 for square roots, which is usually omitted). Simplifying radicals means removing all perfect square factors from the radicand.

To simplify √48, factor the radicand: 48 = 16 × 3 = 4² × 3, so √48 = √(16 × 3) = √16 · √3 = 4√3. Only like radicals (same radicand and same index) can be combined by addition and subtraction, just like combining like terms: 3√5 + 7√5 = 10√5, but 3√2 + 3√3 cannot be combined.

Rationalizing the denominator means removing radicals from the denominator of a fraction. Multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical (or by the conjugate of a binomial denominator). For example, 6/√3 = 6√3/3 = 2√3.
steps: Factor the radicand into a product of perfect squares (or cubes, etc.) and remaining factors
Apply the product rule: √(ab) = √a · √b
Take the square root of the perfect square factor and move it outside the radical
Combine like radicals by adding/subtracting their coefficients
For rationalizing denominators, multiply top and bottom by the radical or conjugate

examples.title: Simplifying √75 + 2√12 − √3
examples.text: √75 = √(25·3) = 5√3. 2√12 = 2√(4·3) = 2·2√3 = 4√3. So: 5√3 + 4√3 − √3 = 8√3. All terms were simplified to like radicals, then combined.

examples.title: Rationalizing 4/(√5 + √2)
examples.text: Multiply by conjugate (√5 − √2)/(√5 − √2): 4(√5 − √2) / [(√5)² − (√2)²] = 4(√5 − √2) / (5 − 2) = 4(√5 − √2) / 3. The denominator is now rational.

lessons.tip: When simplifying radicals, always check for the LARGEST perfect square factor first. For √72, factor: 72 = 36 × 2 (not 9 × 8 → 3√8 which still simplifies). Find the biggest perfect square that divides the radicand to save steps.

quiz.explanation: Like radicals have the same radicand and index. 3√6 and 5√6 both have radicand 6 and index 2.

lessons.title: Rational Expressions & Equations
lessons.description: Master the concepts and applications of rational expressions & equations
lessons.formula:
Simplifying Rational Expressions:
  (a·c)/(b·c) = a/b     (c ≠ 0)

Adding/Subtracting (LCD):
  a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/(bd)

Solving by Cross Multiplication:
  a/b = c/d  →  a·d = b·c

Domain Restrictions:
  Denominator ≠ 0 always!
lessons.content:
A rational expression is a fraction whose numerator and denominator are both polynomials. Like numerical fractions, rational expressions can be simplified, added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided. The key rule is that the denominator can never equal zero — any value that makes the denominator zero is an excluded value and must be removed from the domain.

To simplify a rational expression, factor both numerator and denominator completely, then cancel any common factors (just like reducing fractions: (x² − 9)/(x + 3) = (x+3)(x−3)/(x+3) = x − 3, where x ≠ −3). To add or subtract with different denominators, find the Least Common Denominator (LCD) and rewrite each fraction.

When solving rational equations, multiply both sides by the LCD to clear all fractions, then solve the resulting polynomial equation. Always check your answers in the original equation — solutions that make any denominator zero are extraneous solutions and must be rejected.
steps: Identify all excluded values (set each denominator ≠ 0)
Factor all numerators and denominators completely
Simplify by canceling common factors between numerator and denominator
For equations: multiply both sides by the LCD to clear fractions
Solve the resulting equation and check all solutions against excluded values

examples.title: Simplifying (x² − 4)/(x² + 5x + 6)
examples.text: Factor: numerator = (x+2)(x−2), denominator = (x+2)(x+3). Cancel (x+2): result = (x−2)/(x+3), where x ≠ −2 and x ≠ −3. The excluded value x = −2 was removed during simplification.

examples.title: Solving 3/(x−1) + 2/(x+2) = 1
examples.text: LCD = (x−1)(x+2). Multiply through: 3(x+2) + 2(x−1) = (x−1)(x+2). 3x + 6 + 2x − 2 = x² + x − 2 → 5x + 4 = x² + x − 2. Rearrange: 0 = x² − 4x − 6. Using quadratic formula: x = (4 ± √40)/2 = 2 ± √10. Check: neither value makes a denominator zero, so both are valid.

lessons.tip: The most common mistake is forgetting to check for extraneous solutions. ALWAYS plug your answers back into the original equation. If a solution makes any denominator equal to zero, cross it out and write 'extraneous — rejected.' This step is non-negotiable on tests!

quiz.q: What is the excluded value of x in the expression 5/(x² − 4)?
quiz.explanation: x² − 4 = 0 when x = 2 or x = −2. Both values make the denominator zero, so both are excluded.

quiz.q: After solving a rational equation, a solution is x = −1. The original denominators are x and x+1. What should you do?
options: Reject x = −1 because it makes x+1 = 0
quiz.explanation: x = −1 makes the denominator x + 1 equal to 0, so this is an extraneous solution and must be rejected.

lessons.description: Understand direct variation relationships where y = kx passes through the origin.

y = kx  (k = constant of variation)
Graph: line through origin

lessons.content: Direct variation describes y = kx where k is the constant of variation. The graph is a line through the origin (0,0). When x doubles, y doubles. To test: check that y/x gives the same constant k for every pair. If a linear equation has a y-intercept other than zero (like y = 2x+5), it is NOT direct variation.
steps: Check if equation fits y = kx (no extra constant)

lessons.tip: The litmus test: divide y by x for EVERY data pair — you must get the same k. If any pair gives a different ratio, it's not direct variation.

lessons.title: Quadratic Formula Derivation
lessons.description: Understand where the quadratic formula comes from via completing the square.
lessons.formula:
x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac)) / 2a

Derived by:
1. ax²+bx+c=0, divide by a
2. Move constant, complete square
3. Take square root, solve for x
lessons.content: The quadratic formula x=(−b±√(b²−4ac))/2a is derived by completing the square on ax²+bx+c=0. First divide by a: x²+(b/a)x=−c/a. Add (b/2a)² to both sides. Factor left as (x+b/2a)². Take square root and solve. The discriminant b²−4ac determines solution types: positive→two real, zero→one repeated, negative→two complex.
steps: Divide ax²+bx+c=0 by a
Move c/a to right
Add (b/2a)² to both sides
Factor as perfect square
Take square root (include ±)
Solve for x

examples.title: Full Derivation
examples.text: x²+(b/a)x=−c/a → (x+b/2a)²=(b²−4ac)/4a² → x+b/2a=±√(b²−4ac)/(2a) → x=(−b±√(b²−4ac))/2a

examples.title: Discriminant Analysis
examples.text: 2x²−6x+5: D=36−40=−4<0 → two complex solutions.

lessons.tip: Understanding the derivation is more valuable than memorizing the formula. The same completing-the-square technique appears throughout calculus and statistics.

quiz.explanation: Dividing by a makes leading coefficient 1 for completing the square.

quiz.q: What do you add to complete x²+(b/a)x?
quiz.explanation: For x²+px, add (p/2)². Here p=b/a, so add (b/2a)².

lessons.formula:

If D<0, factor out √(−1)=i
Write x=(−b±i√|D|)/2a
Simplify the fraction

lessons.title: Multiplying Polynomials: The FOIL Method
lessons.description: Multiply two binomials using the FOIL method: First, Outer, Inner, Last.
lessons.formula:
FOIL: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd

First:  a × c
Outer:  a × d
Inner:  b × c
Last:   b × d

Example: (x + 3)(x + 2)
= x² + 2x + 3x + 6
= x² + 5x + 6
lessons.content:
The FOIL method is a handy memory trick for multiplying two binomials (expressions with two terms each). FOIL stands for First, Outer, Inner, Last — the four products you compute. For (x + 3)(x + 2): multiply the First terms (x × x = x²), the Outer terms (x × 2 = 2x), the Inner terms (3 × x = 3x), and the Last terms (3 × 2 = 6). Then add them all together: x² + 2x + 3x + 6 = x² + 5x + 6.

After FOILing, always combine like terms — the middle terms (Outer + Inner) usually combine into one term. In the example above, 2x + 3x = 5x. You can also visualize FOIL using an area model: draw a rectangle divided into four smaller rectangles. Label the sides with each binomial's terms. Each small rectangle's area is one of the FOIL products. The total area of the big rectangle equals the full product. This geometric view helps you see why FOIL works and why you get four separate terms before combining.

Be careful with negative signs! For (2x + 1)(x + 5), the FOIL products are 2x², 10x, x, and 5. Combining the middle terms: 10x + x = 11x, giving 2x² + 11x + 5. For binomials with negatives like (3x − 2)(4x + 3), follow FOIL carefully: First (3x × 4x = 12x²), Outer (3x × 3 = 9x), Inner (−2 × 4x = −8x), Last (−2 × 3 = −6). Combine: 12x² + x − 6. Always slow down on the signs — that's where most mistakes happen!
steps: Write out the two binomials side by side
Multiply the First terms of each binomial
Multiply the Outer terms (left of first × right of second)
Multiply the Inner terms (right of first × left of second)
Multiply the Last terms, then combine like terms to get the final polynomial

examples.title: FOIL: (2x + 1)(x + 5)
examples.text: First: 2x · x = 2x². Outer: 2x · 5 = 10x. Inner: 1 · x = x. Last: 1 · 5 = 5. Combine like terms: 10x + x = 11x. Final answer: 2x² + 11x + 5.

examples.title: FOIL with Negatives: (3x - 2)(4x + 3)
examples.text: First: 3x · 4x = 12x². Outer: 3x · 3 = 9x. Inner: -2 · 4x = -8x. Last: -2 · 3 = -6. Combine: 9x + (-8x) = x. Final answer: 12x² + x - 6.

lessons.tip: Write each of the four FOIL products on a separate line before combining. This prevents errors from trying to do too many steps in your head at once!

quiz.explanation: FOIL: x·x = x², x·2 = 2x, 3·x = 3x, 3·2 = 6. Combine: 2x + 3x = 5x. Answer: x² + 5x + 6.

quiz.q: In FOIL, what does the 'I' stand for?
quiz.explanation: I stands for Inner — multiply the inner terms (right term of the first binomial × left term of the second binomial).
FOIL: x² + x - 4x - 4 = x² - 3x - 4. Inner: -4·x = -4x. Outer: x·1 = x. Combine: x - 4x = -3x.
FOIL: 4x² + 6x + 6x + 9 = 4x² + 12x + 9. This is also a perfect square trinomial: (2x+3)².

lessons.title: Factoring Special Products
lessons.description: Recognize and factor Difference of Squares and Perfect Square Trinomials instantly.
lessons.formula:
Difference of Squares:
a² - b² = (a - b)(a + b)
Examples: x² - 9 = (x-3)(x+3)
4x² - 25 = (2x-5)(2x+5)

Perfect Square Trinomials:
a² + 2ab + b² = (a + b)²
a² - 2ab + b² = (a - b)²
Example: x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)²
lessons.content:
Special products are patterns that appear so frequently in algebra that recognizing them saves enormous time. The first pattern is the Difference of Squares: when you subtract one perfect square from another, like x² − 9, it factors into two conjugate binomials: (x − 3)(x + 3). Notice the middle terms cancel out: −3x + 3x = 0. That's why the result has no 'x' term — only the two squares remain. Examples: 4x² − 25 = (2x − 5)(2x + 5), and 16 − y² = (4 − y)(4 + y).

The second pattern is the Perfect Square Trinomial: these come from squaring a binomial. When you compute (x + 5)², you get x² + 10x + 25. Notice the pattern: the first and last terms are perfect squares (x² and 5² = 25), and the middle term is exactly twice the product of the square roots (2 × x × 5 = 10x). To factor, check: is the first term a square? Is the last term a square? Is the middle term = 2 × √(first) × √(last)? If all three are yes, it's a perfect square trinomial. The sign of the middle term tells you whether to use (a + b)² or (a − b)².

Why memorize these? Because they let you skip the entire FOIL process and factor instantly. When you see x² − 16, you immediately know it's (x − 4)(x + 4). Common mistakes include misidentifying the square roots or forgetting that the sum of squares (like x² + 9) does NOT factor over the reals. Always check: a difference of squares has a MINUS between the terms, never a plus. With practice, these patterns become second nature and dramatically speed up your algebra work.
steps: Identify whether the expression is a Difference of Squares (a² − b²) or a Perfect Square Trinomial (a² ± 2ab + b²)
For Difference of Squares: find the square root of each term (a and b)
Write as (a − b)(a + b) — one plus, one minus
For Perfect Square Trinomials: verify the middle term equals 2ab, then write as (a ± b)²
Always expand your answer to verify it matches the original expression

examples.title: Factoring a Difference of Squares: x² - 25
examples.text: x² − 25 = x² − 5² = (x − 5)(x + 5). Both terms are perfect squares, separated by subtraction. The square roots are x and 5, giving conjugate factors (x−5) and (x+5).

examples.title: Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial: x² + 10x + 25
examples.text: First term: x² (square root x). Last term: 25 (square root 5). Middle term: 10x = 2·x·5 ✓. It matches the pattern a² + 2ab + b², so x² + 10x + 25 = (x + 5)².

lessons.tip: To check for a perfect square trinomial, take the square root of the first and last terms, multiply them, double the result, and see if it matches the middle term. If it does, you've found your pattern!

quiz.explanation: x² - 16 = x² - 4² = (x - 4)(x + 4). This is a difference of squares pattern.
√(x²) = x, √(9) = 3, and 2·x·3 = 6x matches the middle term. So x² + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)².

quiz.q: Which expression is a Difference of Squares?
quiz.explanation: 4x² - 49 = (2x)² - 7² is a difference of two perfect squares. It factors as (2x - 7)(2x + 7).

quiz.q: Can x² + 4 be factored over the real numbers?
options: No — it's a sum of squares, not a difference
quiz.explanation: x² + 4 is a sum of squares, not a difference of squares. Sum of squares cannot be factored over the real numbers.
